abstract: "Mental rotation — the ability to mentally transform an object's orientation in space — is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive psychology, yet evidence for its cross-cultural validity in children remains limited. We examined performance on the LEVANTE (Learning Variability Network Exchange) mental rotation task across three international study sites (Colombia, Germany, and Canada)  in 1,037 children aged 5--13 years. The task demonstrated measurement invariance across all three sites (2PL scalar invariance model; ΔBIC = 216.4 vs. best Rasch model). The angular disparity effect (Shepard & Metzler, 1971) replicated robustly for 3D stimuli (β = 0.19, p < .001), with a 90° increase in rotation angle associated with approximately 45% longer response times; the effect was present but attenuated for 2D stimuli (β = 0.16, p < .001). No main effect of sex was detected (β = -0.03, p = .94). Exploratory clustering identified three engagement profiles: Mental Rotation (monotonically increasing RT–angle function), Other Effective Strategies (feature matching/flipping), and Ineffective Strategies (absent angular sensitivity, low ability). These findings establish that the task captures a consistent, spatially-driven construct across culturally diverse samples — a necessary precondition for using cross-cultural data to understand variation in spatial reasoning."

# Introduction
From fitting puzzle pieces together at age three to navigating complex diagrams in school, spatial reasoning underpins a broad array of cognitive achievements — and children differ substantially as individuals in how these skills develop.
Such variability is detectable early, across a wide range of spatial tasks in primary school-aged children [@hodgkiss2021developmental; @lauer2019development], and its consequences are far-reaching: spatial ability predicts outcomes spanning creative domains such as music [@padulo2020effects; @hetland2000learning] and the visual arts [@kell2013creativity; @winner2013relationship], mathematical achievement [@gunderson2012relation], science learning [@gilligan2020first], and long-term educational and occupational outcomes in STEM fields [@wai2009spatial]. Understanding what drives this variability is therefore a question of both theoretical and practical importance. The present study takes a step toward that goal by examining children's performance on a mental rotation task across three international study sites, asking both what is consistent across cultures and what varies.

Spatial reasoning encompasses abilities for representing, transforming, and reasoning about visuospatial information [@lohman1996spatial]. Rather than a single unified capacity, it is better understood as a family of related but distinguishable skills, including mental rotation, spatial visualization, perspective-taking, and navigation, that differ in the type of spatial information involved and the cognitive operations required [@uttal2013malleability; @newcombe2018three]. These skills can be organized along two dimensions: whether the spatial relations are intrinsic to an object or extrinsic between objects, and whether the task requires dynamic mental transformation or only static representation [@uttal2013malleability]. Mental rotation — the focus of the present study — falls in the intrinsic-dynamic quadrant of this framework, involving the mental transformation of a single object's orientation in space.

The classic mental rotation tasks, first developed by @shepard1971mental, presents participants with pairs of objects at varying angular disparities and asks them to judge whether the objects are identical or mirror-reversed, with response time and accuracy as the key dependent variables. It is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive psychology. The dominant account of how people solve it — 'pure' or analog rotation — holds that the solver constructs a holistic mental image of the object and continuously rotates it until it aligns with the target. Because the mental image must traverse each intermediate angle, larger rotations take proportionally longer [@shepard1971mental; @cooper1973chronometric]. The result is one of the most robust and replicable findings in the field: response times increase approximately linearly with angular disparity (i.e., how far an object has been rotated from its original orientation).

The original paradigm used 3D block figures, and adult research has predominantly followed suit. Developmental research, however, has tended to use simpler 2D stimuli — animal silhouettes or abstract shapes — on the grounds that 3D figures may be too demanding for younger children [@jansen2013mental], and studies of spatial development in middle childhood have mainly relied on 2D stimuli [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. As a result, the adult and child literatures have largely developed in parallel, and whether the angular disparity effect holds comparably for 2D and 3D stimuli across the primary school years remains poorly understood. The LEVANTE task offers an opportunity to examine this directly, as it includes both stimulus types within the same paradigm across a broad developmental window. 

Beyond stimulus type, the linear RT–angle relationship shown by @shepard1971mental may itself obscure meaningful individual variation in the processes underlying performance. For example, performance on the task may not necessarily reflect mental rotation per se, as participants may instead rely on alternative spatial strategies that produce similar accuracy and response time patterns. Research with adults suggests that solvers draw on a range of strategies, spanning a holistic-analytic continuum [@gluck2003spatial]. At the holistic end, solvers use 'pure' or analog rotation as described above. Feature-based strategies, by contrast, operate by identifying discrete local features — a particular arm, corner, or protrusion — and rotating or comparing these components rather than rotating the whole object [@just1985cognitive; @khooshabeh2013individual]. A related approach, 'flipping', involves mentally reflecting one object along an axis to check for mirror symmetry, again engaging a different type of spatial transformation. Because these approaches decompose the problem into parts, they can produce correct responses even when the angular disparity effect is attenuated or absent — making them distinguishable from analog rotation at the level of RT patterns. Importantly, this distinction concerns process, not proficiency: feature-based strategies draw on genuine spatial ability, they simply engage it differently [@hegarty2018ability]. More recent work suggests that solvers do not consistently adopt a single strategy but instead shift flexibly between holistic and feature based approaches depending on the demands of a particular item [@nazareth2019strategy].

Importantly, far less is known about which strategies children employ when solving mental rotation problems, and whether strategy use varies with age, ability, or cultural context. Recent work by @mckee2025malleability finds that children rely on non-rotation strategies — flipping and feature matching — more often than analog rotation, with strategy choice shaped by how the task is framed. This question motivates the exploratory component of the present study, which we describe below. These questions take on added significance given how narrow the populations studied to date have been.

Mental rotation ability develops across a prolonged period from infancy through adolescence. Precursors of successful rotation are detectable in the first year of life [@frick2014development; @moore2008mental], and performance on explicit rotation tasks improves substantially between ages 3--13 years [@frick2013development; @marmor1975development; @kail1980developmental], with continued refinement into adolescence. This extended developmental trajectory makes the primary school years, ages 5--13 years, a particularly informative window for studying how mental rotation skills are acquired and how they vary across children.

One prominent source of variation is child sex.^[We refer to sex differences throughout (in the sense of the biological variable), though some observed differences may reflect gender-related factors such as socialization and experience. We remain agnostic about this question here.] Sex differences in mental rotation are well documented in adults [@voyer1995magnitude; @zell2015evaluating], but in children the picture is considerably less clear. @lauer2019development synthesized data from over 30,000 children aged 3--17, finding no reliable sex difference in the preschool years, a small male advantage emerging around age 6 (g ≈ 0.20), and a moderate effect only by age 14, with task and stimulus characteristics explaining substantial variability independently of age. This sensitivity to stimulus type and age has been documented most systematically in German primary school children. The gap is typically absent in younger children and emerges around age 10, concentrated in more demanding cube figure conditions — particularly for girls, who show less improvement across grades than boys [@neuburger2011gender; @jansen2013mental]. However, the direction of the difference can reverse entirely under female-congruent stimulus conditions [@ruthsatz2017gender; @ruthsatz2019girls]. Evidence from other countries is similarly inconsistent: male advantages have been reported in Italian children from age 8 [@moe2018mental], in Dutch children aged 7–9 though not in older children in the same sample [@van2019sex], and in French children at age 11–12 but not at 7–8 [@hoyek2011use]. In contrast, no significant sex difference was found across the full primary school age range in a UK sample [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. Whether these discrepancies reflect genuine cultural variation, differences in task format, or both remains unclear.

The vast majority of developmental research on mental rotation has been conducted with children in middle-to-high-income Western convenience populations [@henrich2010weirdest], raising questions about whether findings about its developmental trajectory, psychometric properties, and underlying cognitive processes generalize beyond the populations in which they were established.

The limited cross-cultural evidence that does exist spans different populations, developmental periods, and spatial tasks, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how cultural context shapes performance. Studies with children from two small-scale societies — including Tsimané forager-horticulturalists in Bolivia [@davis2019spatial] and seminomadic pastoralist-forager children in northern Namibia [@davis2021cultural] — have focused primarily on broader spatial skills rather than mental rotation specifically. In one of the few studies to examine mental rotation cross-culturally in children, researchers compared children in the Ivory Coast and Switzerland and found that the overall shape of the RT–angle curve was similar across both groups, suggesting the basic mental rotation signature is present in both cultural contexts [@nunez1998mental]. However, age predicted performance in the Swiss group but not the Ivorian group, pointing to the possibility that the developmental trajectory of mental rotation differs across cultures even when its basic signature holds. Yet the study has important limitations — it was small (n = 151) and relied on a computerized task likely more familiar to Swiss children. Notably, the authors themselves attributed much of the observed RT difference to cultural differences in familiarity with technology and the value placed on speed, rather than to differences in spatial cognition per se. Taken together, the cross-cultural validity of the mental rotation paradigm with children remains largely unestablished.

Review of the existing work on mental rotation suggests three gaps. First, we have limited data on whether mental rotation tasks developed and validated in resource-rich contexts measure the same underlying construct when administered to children from different cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds. Second, even where cross-cultural comparisons have been made, they have rarely examined whether performance shows the same characteristic patterns across contexts. The linear relationship between reaction time and angular disparity has been demonstrated repeatedly in middle-to-high-income Western samples of children and adults [@kaltner2016developmental; @jansen2015role], but its replication across varied international sites remains largely untested. Third, whether and when sex differences in mental rotation emerge in primary school children remains unclear, with findings varying substantially across studies and tasks — making it a natural question to examine in a cross-cultural dataset. Beyond these three gaps, relatively little is known about the cognitive strategies children employ when solving mental rotation problems, and whether these vary across cultural contexts — a question we explore tentatively here. We address these gaps with four sets of analyses, corresponding to four research questions, each building toward a broader understanding of how and why children's spatial reasoning varies across cultures.

## The Present Study
The present study uses data from the Learning Variability Network Exchange (LEVANTE), an international research collaboration designed to capture how children's learning and development vary across ages and cultural contexts. LEVANTE's central aim is to build a large, openly shared dataset of children's cognitive development across diverse settings, with a particular focus on individual variability — what differs across children, and why. Data were collected from three geographically and culturally diverse pilot sites: the Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá and nearby rural areas, Colombia (uniandes-co); the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany (mpieva-de); and the University of Western Ontario in London, Canada (western-ca). Here we use data from a single task in the LEVANTE battery: a mental rotation task designed and scored using an item response theory measurement approach, which allows directly comparable ability estimates to be derived across children who completed different subsets of items [@Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks]. LEVANTE is not designed to support site-level performance comparisons — sites vary substantially in sampling, recruitment, and test administration in ways that heavily confound absolute comparisons. Differences in overall scores across sites should therefore not be interpreted as reflecting population differences. However, examining the consistency of patterns within each site can still be informative, and this is the approach we take here.

Our first research question asks whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task achieves measurement invariance across three international study sites — that is, whether the task captures the same underlying construct regardless of where it is administered. Our second asks whether reaction time performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli, as originally demonstrated by @shepard1971mental, using the angular disparity effect as the key benchmark: as the angular difference between two objects increases, so too should the time required to judge whether they match. If children across three culturally diverse sites show this same systematic pattern, this constitutes good evidence that the task is engaging the spatial demands it was designed to capture. Our third research question asks whether a sex difference in mental rotation is detectable in this sample, and whether it interacts with age. Alongside these three primary research questions, we tentatively explore a fourth: whether children draw on different cognitive strategies when solving mental rotation problems, and whether their strategies vary across contexts. These four questions move from psychometric structure (*Cross-Site Invariance*), to process-level validity (*Angular Sensitivity*), to individual variation (*Sex Differences*), to profiles of engagement (*Strategy Variation*) — building a layered case for the task's cross-cultural validity.

```{r}
#| label: filter-runs

# apply filters to runs for use in all subsequent analyses
min_trials <- 10
min_gap_months <- 3
run_data_filtered <- run_data |>
  filter(num_attempted >= min_trials) |>
  filter(!is.na(age), age >= 5, age <= 14) |>
  arrange(user_id, age) |>
  group_by(user_id) |>
  mutate(run_number = row_number(),
         age_gap = age - lag(age)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter_out(age_gap < min_gap_months / 12) |>
  select(site, user_id, run_id, age, adaptive)

# create age groups based on roughly equal sample sizes
n_groups <- 3
ages <- run_data_filtered |> pull(age)
age_breaks <- quantile(ages, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_groups + 1))

# add age groups and site labels
runs_filtered <- run_data_filtered |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age, breaks = age_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE),
         site_label = site |>
           recode_values(from = site_labels, to = names(site_labels)))
```

```{r}
#| label: sample-counts

# overall
site_n <- run_data |>
  filter(!is.na(age), age >= 5, age <= 14) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(n_users = n_distinct(user_id))

n_uniandes <- site_n |> filter(site == "uniandes-co") |> pull(n_users)
n_mpieva <- site_n |> filter(site == "mpieva-de")  |> pull(n_users)
n_western <- site_n |> filter(site == "western-ca") |> pull(n_users)

mrot_df <- mrot_scores |>
  inner_join(runs_filtered)

n_excluded <- mrot_scores |>
  anti_join(mrot_df) |>
  summarise(n_users = n_distinct(user_id),
            n_runs = n_distinct(run_id))

n_final <- mrot_df |>
  summarise(n_users = n_distinct(user_id),
            n_runs = n_distinct(run_id))

n_repeat_users <- runs_filtered %>%
  group_by(user_id) %>%
  summarise(n_assessments = n_distinct(run_id)) %>%
  filter(n_assessments > 1) %>%
  nrow()
```
# Methods

## Participants
Data were drawn from three LEVANTE pilot sites: Universidad de los Andes, Bogotá and nearby rural areas, Colombia (uniandes-co); Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig, Germany (mpieva-de); and the University of Western Ontario, London, Canada (western-ca). Site codes rather than country names are used throughout to reflect that each site represents a single institution/region within a large, diverse country, and should not be taken as representative of national populations.

### uniandes-co
The Universidad de los Andes site (uniandes-co) recruited `r n_uniandes` children aged 5--13 years across six schools in Colombia: four in Bogotá — three affiliated with family compensation funds and one managed by a charter school organisation — and two public schools in the rural departments of Caquetá (i.e., in a municipality located northeast of Florencia) and Boyacá (i.e., in a municipality close to Chiquinquira).  Bogota is the largest and most populous city in Colombia, with a population of over seven million individuals residing within the urban area [@statsco], and substantial variation in socioeconomic status [@statsco]. Florencia and Chiquinquira are smaller municipalities with populations of over 150,000 individuals and 50,000 individuals respectively [@statsco]. Children were recruited from schools with existing partnerships with the Universidad de los Andes. Data were collected in groups using tablets provided by the research team, with group size altered for the age of the children (smaller groups for younger children). Due to time constraints inherent to school-based administration, children typically completed a subset of tasks.

### mpieva-de
The Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology site (mpieva-de) collected data from `r n_mpieva` children aged 5--13 years in Leipzig, Germany. Leipzig a mid-sized urban centre with a population of approximately 600,000 individuals [@statsde], and participants in the current study mainly came from middle- to upper-middle-income backgrounds. Children and their families were recruited from an existing database of Leipzig residents via telephone and completed tasks remotely at home using their own devices. 

### western-ca
The Western University site (western-ca) recruited `r n_western` children aged 5--13 years primarily from London, Ontario, with a smaller number from the Greater Toronto Area. London is a medium-sized urban and suburban area with a population of over 400,000 individuals [@statscan]. The Greater Toronto Area is a large urban and suburban area, comprising the city of Toronto and four surrounding regional municipalities, and is the most population metropolitan region in Canada with a population of over 6 million individuals [@statscan]. Canadian participants in the current study mainly came from middle- to upper-middle-income backgrounds. Recruitment relied on online outreach through social media and community groups, supplemented by local posters and school newsletters. Children were assessed individually by a researcher in a dedicated campus testing space. 

Site-level sampling characteristics are described in @tbl-participants. Due to de-identification protocols, individual-level demographic data — including socioeconomic indicators — are not available for the current sample. `r n_excluded$n_runs` assessments (from `r n_excluded$n_users` participants) were excluded due to missing age, being outside the target age range (5--13 years), having too few trials (<`r min_trials`), or having too short a gap between administrations (<`r min_gap_months` months), leaving a final sample of n = `r n_final$n_runs` assessments (from `r n_final$n_users` participants). A total of `r n_repeat_users` children contributed two assessments each; each assessment was treated as a separate observation, with participant included as a random effect in all mixed-effects models to account for the non-independence of repeated assessments. Data and analysis code for this paper are available at <https://github.com/levante-framework/mental-rotation>. For more information about LEVANTE public data releases, see <https://researcher.levante-network.org/data>.

```{r}
#| label: trial-level-rts

mrot_rt_trial <- task_data |>
  select(site, data) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  inner_join(runs_filtered) |>
  select(site, site_label, user_id, run_id, adaptive, age, age_group, trial_id,
         trial_number, item_uid, item_group, item, item_original, correct, rt_numeric) |>
  mutate(
    correct    = as.integer(correct),
    rt_s       = as.numeric(rt_numeric) / 1000,
    log_rt     = log(rt_s),
    angle      = as.integer(stringr::str_extract(item, "(?<=_)\\d+")),
    angle_full = as.integer(stringr::str_extract(item_original, "\\d{3}$")),
    stimulus   = str_extract(item, "^[a-z]+")
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(rt_s), rt_s > 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: cat-exclusion-counts

cat_counts <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  group_by(adaptive) |>
  summarise(trials = n(), runs = n_distinct(run_id)) |>
  mutate(adaptive = if_else(adaptive, "n_cat", "n_non_cat")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(trials, runs), names_to = "count") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = adaptive, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(n_total = n_cat + n_non_cat,
         pct_cat = round(n_cat / n_total * 100, 1)) |>
  nest(counts = -count) |>
  deframe()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-participants
#| tbl-cap: "**Participant/assessment characteristics by site.** Age in years."

trials_per_run <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  group_by(site_label, user_id, run_id) %>%
  summarise(n_trials = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(site_label) %>%
  summarise(
    trials_mean = mean(n_trials, na.rm = TRUE),
    trials_min  = min(n_trials, na.rm = TRUE),
    trials_max  = max(n_trials, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(trials_summary = sprintf("%.0f [%d–%d]", trials_mean, trials_min, trials_max)) |>
  select(site_label, trials_summary)

site_info <- mrot_df |>
  # distinct(user_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  group_by(site_label) |>
  summarise(
    n_run    = n(),
    n_user   = n_distinct(user_id),
    age_mean = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_sd   = sd(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_min  = min(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_max  = max(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    age_summary = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f) [%.1f–%.1f]",
                          age_mean, age_sd, age_min, age_max),
    testing_format =  case_when(
      site_label == "uniandes-co" ~ "In school; group; tablet (researcher-provided)",
      site_label == "mpieva-de"   ~ "Remote (home-based); individual; family device",
      site_label == "western-ca"  ~ "On-campus; individual; tablet (researcher-provided)"
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(trials_per_run) |>
  select(Site = site_label,
         `N assessments` = n_run,
         `N participants` = n_user,
```

## Measure
The nine core tasks in the LEVANTE battery, including mental rotation, were initially designed in English and then subsequently adapted for Spanish and German following a set of internationalization procedures in collaboration with researchers at the uniandes-co and mpieva-de sites, respectively. The LEVANTE mental rotation task [@frick2013development] is administered digitally on a tablet or computer as part of a battery of nine core tasks. It employs two stimulus categories of increasing difficulty: 2D animal figures (ducks and rabbits), and 3D block configurations from the @shepard1971mental set (see [Appendix A (Example Items)](#sec-apx-mrot-example-items). On each trial, a target image is displayed alongside two alternatives: one shows the same object rotated to a different angle, and the other is a mirror-reversed version that cannot be matched to the target by rotation alone. Children select whichever alternative they judge to correspond to the target by tapping or clicking on their device. The angular disparity between target and correct alternative varies systematically across trials (ranging from 20° to 360°), enabling examination of how increasing rotation demands affect both accuracy and response latency.

### Computer-Adaptive Testing Format
The LEVANTE team has implemented the mental rotation task in a computer-adaptive testing (CAT) format. In the adaptive version, participant ability is summarized by a latent proficiency estimate (θ) that is re-estimated after each response. The updated θ then guides selection of the next item so that it is appropriately challenging for each individual child. This trial-by-trial targeting typically makes the task more engaging and increases measurement efficiency, enabling reliable ability estimation with fewer administered items. In the present sample, `r cat_counts$runs$pct_cat`% of administrations (`r cat_counts$runs$n_cat` of `r cat_counts$runs$n_total`) used the CAT format. In the fixed format, testing stopped after either six consecutive incorrect responses or a maximum of 10 minutes, whichever came first. Refer to @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks for more information on the internationalization procedures and CAT versions of all LEVANTE tasks.

## Analysis

### Item Screening
Prior to fitting psychometric models, we examined item-level performance within each site to identify poorly functioning items. Items were screened for having average accuracy near or below chance, low item–total correlations, high missingness, or other anomalous patterns – as a result no items were identified as warranting exclusion from further analysis for this task. For full details of the item screening procedure, see @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks.

### Item Response Theory Models
Item response theory (IRT) is a psychometric framework that models the relationship between a latent trait and performance on individual task items. Unlike classical test theory, which relies on total scores and treats all items as equivalent contributors to measurement, IRT estimates item-level parameters independently of the specific sample tested, providing more precise measurement across the ability range. All models assumed a single underlying factor, following standard practice in psychometric analyses of mental rotation tasks and consistent with the task's design as a measure of a single spatial ability.

We compared two types of IRT models. The Rasch model (1-parameter logistic; 1PL) estimates only item difficulty, holding discrimination constant across items — that is, it assumes all items are equally good at differentiating children of higher versus lower ability. The two-parameter logistic model (2PL) relaxes this constraint, additionally estimating each item's discrimination parameter. A better-fitting 2PL therefore indicates that items vary meaningfully in how well they distinguish between ability levels.

### Analysis 1: Cross-Site Invariance
To assess cross-site measurement invariance, we fitted both types of models with varying constraints across the three sites: configural invariance (all parameters free to vary), metric invariance (item discriminations are constrained to be equal), and scalar invariance (both discriminations and difficulties are constrained to be equal). We compared models using BIC (Bayesian information criterion) as the selection criterion [@putnick2016measurement].
<!-- Overlapping items across sites served as anchors to establish a common scale, with non-overlapping items freely estimated within the same multigroup model. -->
<!-- MB: removed above sentence because all items overlap in this task -->
We estimated all models in R using the mirt package [@chalmers2012mirt] via marginal maximum likelihood with 500 quadrature points. We specified Gaussian priors on item difficulty ($\mathcal{N}(0,3)$) and discrimination ($\mathcal{N}(1,0.3)$) in all models. We extracted ability scores (θ) using expected a posteriori (EAP) scoring.

### Analysis 2: Angular Sensitivity
To investigate whether performance was sensitive to rotation angle as originally demonstrated by @shepard1971mental, we fitted linear mixed-effects models predicting log response time (RT) from rotation angle, with participant level intercepts and slopes for angle. Warm-up trials (20°) were excluded, leaving rotation angles ranging from 40° to 360°.
For analysis, rotation angles were recoded to their shortest-path equivalents, collapsing the full 0–360° range to angular disparities of 0–180° (e.g., a 320° rotation was treated as a 40° disparity), on the assumption that participants take the most efficient rotational path. This recoding was verified in a robustness check using full 0–360° angles reported in [Appendix D (360° Angle Functions)](#sec-apx-360-angle). Rotation angle was standardized (M = 0, SD = 1) prior to analysis. We fitted separate models for 2D and 3D stimuli. For each, we additionally tested site as a moderator of the angle slope by including a site × angle interaction. A combined model including both stimulus types was used to test whether the angle slope differed between 2D and 3D items. Only correct trials were included in RT analyses. CAT trials were excluded from RT models because adaptive item selection produces non-random angle exposure: higher-ability children disproportionately receive high-angle items and lower-ability children receive low-angle items. This correlation between ability and angle makes it impossible to obtain unbiased estimates of the RT–angle relationship, regardless of whether angular sensitivity itself varies with ability. Of `r cat_counts$trials$n_total` trials from all assessments, `r cat_counts$trials$n_cat` (`r cat_counts$trials$pct_cat`%) were administered in CAT format and excluded, leaving `r cat_counts$trials$n_non_cat` trials for this analysis. 

### Analysis 3: Sex Differences
To examine whether IRT-based ability scores differed by sex, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model predicting ability scores from sex, age, and their interaction, with fixed effects for site and random intercepts for participant. Fixed rather than random site effects were used given the small number of sites (k = 3). Sex at birth was reported by caregivers as part of the LEVANTE background survey.

### Analysis 4: Strategy Variation
To characterize individual differences in how children engaged with the task's spatial demands, we first fitted a mixed-effects model predicting log RT from rotation angle, stimulus type, their interaction, and trial number, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for angle and trial number, and a random intercept by item. Unlike the angular sensitivity analysis, CAT trials were retained here and both correct and incorrect trials were included: the strategy analysis extracts relative person-level features rather than estimating the angle effect at the population level, and including all available trials (correct and incorrect) yields more reliable individual-level estimates.

From this model, we extracted five person-level features for each child. Baseline response speed reflects general processing efficiency independent of rotation demands. Angular sensitivity was captured two ways: as the absolute RT–angle slope (the time added per degree of rotation), and as that slope expressed relative to each child's baseline speed, capturing the degree to which rotation demands slow a child down proportional to their typical pace — a relative measure better suited to a developmental sample where baseline processing speed varies substantially with age. The trial-by-trial RT trend indexes within-session learning or fatigue. Finally, response instability captures trial-to-trial variability that cannot be attributed to angle or trial position — children who disengage from the task's spatial demands or shift inconsistently between approaches are expected to show greater residual variability than those applying a consistent strategy; this was operationalized as the standard deviation of model residuals. Each feature was retained on the basis that it captures a distinct and interpretable aspect of how children engage with the task's spatial demands. These five features were submitted to k-means clustering as a descriptive tool to identify broad patterns of engagement.

## Analysis 1: Cross-Site Invariance

```{r}
#| label: mrot-irt-values

mrot_2pl_scalar <- mrot_models %>%
  filter(task == "mrot", itemtype == "2pl", invariance == "scalar")

mrot_2pl_configural <- mrot_models %>%
  filter(task == "mrot", itemtype == "2pl", invariance == "configural")

mrot_rasch_scalar <- mrot_models %>%
  filter(task == "mrot", itemtype == "rasch", invariance == "scalar")

delta_bic_rasch <- round(mrot_rasch_scalar$BIC - mrot_2pl_scalar$BIC, 1)
delta_bic_configural <- round(mrot_2pl_configural$BIC - mrot_2pl_scalar$BIC, 1)
bic_2pl_scalar  <- round(mrot_2pl_scalar$BIC, 2)
aic_2pl_scalar  <- round(mrot_2pl_scalar$AIC, 2)
npar_2pl_scalar <- mrot_2pl_scalar$df
```

Our first research question asked whether the task measured the mental rotation construct in the same way across all three sites — that is, whether it achieves measurement invariance. The 2PL scalar invariance model provided the best fit (BIC = `r bic_2pl_scalar`, AIC = `r aic_2pl_scalar`, *k* = `r npar_2pl_scalar`), outperforming the 2PL configural invariance model by `r delta_bic_configural` BIC points and the Rasch scalar invariance model by `r delta_bic_rasch` BIC points (see @tbl-mrot-irt).

The better fit of the 2PL model compared to the Rasch model indicates that mental rotation items vary in their discrimination — specifically, items with higher angular disparity provide more information at higher abilities. In addition to the 2PL model being favored over the Rasch model in terms of model fit, it also provides substantially higher marginal reliabilities (2PL: `r rxx[["2pl"]]`; Rasch: `r rxx$rasch`), providing further support for its suitability.

Crucially, scalar invariance was supported over more flexible alternatives, meaning that both item discriminations and difficulties were equivalent across sites — items are not only ordered similarly in difficulty across sites, but the absolute spacing between them on the latent scale is also preserved. This means that children across sites are being measured on a comparable scale, and that differences in θ are not attributable to site-specific measurement artifacts. Practically, the relative difficulty and discrimination of items — for example, the greater challenge posed by larger rotation angles and 3D figures — is consistent in magnitude across study sites, and ability estimates can be placed on a common latent scale [@putnick2016measurement].

Scalar invariance is a psychometric property of the instrument: it establishes that scores can be meaningfully compared across contexts, but does not by itself speak to what cognitive process is driving performance. Evidence that children are engaging the spatial demands the task was designed to capture — specifically, the predicted increase in response time with angular disparity — is addressed in Analysis 2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mrot-irt
#| tbl-cap: "**Model fit indices for IRT models fit to overlapping items.** Note: 2PL = 2-parameter logistic model; Rasch model constrains all item discriminations to be equal. Configural invariance allows all parameters to vary across groups; metric constrains discriminations across groups; scalar constrains discriminations and difficulties. The selected model (bold) had the lowest BIC."

best_row <- which.min(mrot_models$BIC)

invar_table <- mrot_models %>%
  # transmute(
  #   Model       = itemtype %>% fct_recode("Rasch" = "rasch", "2PL" = "2pl"),
  #   Invariance  = invariance,
  #   `Log-likelihood` = logLik,
  #   AIC         = AIC,
  #   BIC         = BIC,
  #   Parameters  = df,
  #   model_order = model_order
  # ) %>%
  mutate(itemtype = itemtype %>% fct_recode("Rasch" = "rasch", "2PL" = "2pl")) %>%
  mutate(dBIC = BIC - lag(BIC)) %>%
  select(itemtype, invariance, logLik, AIC, BIC, dBIC, df, model_order) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = md("")) %>%
  cols_hide(columns = model_order) %>%
  cols_label(itemtype = "Model",
             invariance = "Invariance",
             logLik = "Log-likelihood",
             dBIC = "ΔBIC",
             df = "ΔParameters") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(logLik, AIC, BIC, dBIC), decimals = 2) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = df, decimals = 0, use_seps = FALSE) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(itemtype, invariance, df)) %>%
  cols_align(align = "right",  columns = c(logLik, AIC, BIC)) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_text(weight = "bold"),
      cell_fill(color = "#f0f7ff")
    ),
    locations = cells_body(rows = best_row)
  ) %>%
  # tab_footnote(
  #   footnote = "Degrees of freedom not computed for the baseline configural model.",
  #   locations = cells_body(columns = df, 
  #                          rows = itemtype == "Rasch" & itemtype == "configural")
  # ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Computed relative to the previous model in the sequence.",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = c(dBIC, df))
  ) %>%
  tab_row_group(label = "2PL",   rows = model_order %in% 3:5) %>%
  tab_row_group(label = "Rasch", rows = model_order %in% 1:2) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    data_row.padding = px(3),
    row_group.font.weight = "bold"
  )
invar_table
```

```{r}
plot_scatter <- function(data, x_var, y_var, x_lab, y_lab) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[x_var]], y = .data[[y_var]],
                   label = item_label)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1,
                linetype = "dashed", colour = pal$grey) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 2.8, family = .font,
                    max.overlaps = Inf,
                    box.padding = 0.5,
                    point.padding = 0.3,
                    na.rm = TRUE) +
    # coord_equal(xlim = c(-2.5, 4), ylim = c(-2.5, 4)) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = x_lab, y = y_lab)
}
```

```{r}
co_bogota_age_sd   <- co_age_summary |> filter(co_site == "uniandes-co-bogota") |> pull(age_sd)   |> round(1)
co_rural_age_mean  <- co_age_summary |> filter(co_site == "uniandes-co-rural")  |> pull(age_mean) |> round(1)
co_rural_age_sd    <- co_age_summary |> filter(co_site == "uniandes-co-rural")  |> pull(age_sd)   |> round(1)

# best-fitting model BIC for by-dataset model
co_dataset_best_bic <- task_anova_both |>
  filter(model_set == "multigroup_dataset") |>
  slice_min(BIC) |>
  pull(BIC) |>
  round(2)

co_dataset_bic <- task_anova_both |>
  filter(model_set == "multigroup_dataset") |>
  select(invariance, BIC) |>
  deframe()

co_dataset_best_invariance <- task_anova_both |>
  filter(model_set == "multigroup_dataset") |>
  slice_min(BIC) |>
  pull(invariance)

# adaptive split
co_bogota_pct_nonadaptive <- co_adaptive |> 
  filter(co_site == "uniandes-co-bogota", adaptive == FALSE) |> 
  pull(pct)

co_rural_pct_adaptive <- co_adaptive |>
  filter(co_site == "uniandes-co-rural", adaptive == TRUE) |>
  pull(pct)
```


### Analysis 1a: Within-site grouping
The uniandes-co site recruited children across both urban schools in Bogotá and rural schools in Caquetá and Boyacá, raising the question of whether the scalar invariance result holds when these two sub-samples are treated as distinct groups. To examine this, we refit the multigroup IRT models with uniandes-co split into two datasets (uniandes-co-bogota, n = `r co_bogota_n`; uniandes-co-rural, n = `r co_rural_n`) rather than pooled as a single site. `r stringr::str_to_sentence(co_dataset_best_invariance)` invariance remained the best-fitting model by BIC (BIC = `r co_dataset_bic[["scalar"]]` for scalar, `r co_dataset_bic[["metric"]]` for metric, `r co_dataset_bic[["configural"]]` for configural), indicating that item parameters are consistent across the two uniandes-co sub-samples as well as across the three main sites. Item difficulty estimates under a configural model were largely consistent across uniandes-co-bogota and uniandes-co-rural for both 2D and 3D items, with the exception of the estimate for one 3D item at the highest rotation angle in uniandes-co-bogota, which likely reflects estimation instability rather than a genuine difference 
(see [Appendix B (Uniandes-co Rural and Urban Sub-samples)](#sec-apx-co-rural-urban)). Age distributions across the two uniandes-co sub-samples were also comparable (uniandes-co-bogota: M = `r co_bogota_age_mean`, SD = `r co_bogota_age_sd`; uniandes-co-rural: M = `r co_rural_age_mean`, SD = `r co_rural_age_sd`).
<!-- indicating that the invariance result is not driven by age composition differences. -->
These results support treating uniandes-co as a single group in the main analysis.

### Analysis 1b: Age Sensitivity
Scalar invariance establishes structural equivalence across sites, but does not on its own confirm that θ reflects meaningful variation in mental rotation ability. As a check on construct validity, @fig-ability-age shows participants' IRT-estimated ability (θ) against age, with GAM (generalized additive model)-smoothed trends shown as a visualization aid to highlight the general shape of developmental trajectories without imposing a linear form; formal statistical modeling of these trends is reported in @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks. Across all three sites, ability increases with age, confirming that the task is sensitive to developmental change — a prerequisite for the individual-differences analyses that follow. The dispersion of points within age bands also underscores the substantial individual variability among same-aged children that motivates our strategy analysis. Note that level differences between site trajectories reflect differences in sample composition and should not be interpreted as cross-cultural differences in ability.

```{r}
#| label: rt-angle-lme

# filter to non-CAT, add age group, stimulus, angle
mrot_lme_data <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  filter(!adaptive, correct == 1) %>%
  mutate(
    item_group = factor(item_group) |> fct_relevel("3d"), # 2D vs 3D
    site       = factor(site),
    angle_sc   = as.numeric(scale(angle)), 
  )
```

```{r}
# check size

# fit all models on the same object
m_3d_main <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_sc + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
  data = mrot_3d, REML = FALSE,

)

)

)

anova_3d <- anova(m_3d_main, m_3d_site, m_3d_age, m_3d_full)

)

)
```

## Analysis 2: Angular Sensitivity
Our second research question asked whether trial-level performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli — specifically, whether the angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental replicates across all three sites. A total of `r n_children_3d` children contributed 3D trials (M age = `r age_3d_mean`, SD = `r age_3d_sd`, range = `r age_3d_min`--`r age_3d_max` years). For 3D stimuli, there was a strong positive effect of rotation angle (β = `r round(beta_3d_main, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_3d_main, 2)`, t(`r round(df_3d_main, 1)`) = `r round(t_3d_main, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_3d_main)`), confirming that response times increased systematically with angular disparity across the full sample. This effect corresponds to a 90-degree increase in rotation angle being associated with approximately `r pct_increase_90`% longer response times for 3D stimuli. Adding site as a moderator significantly improved model fit (χ²(`r anova_site_df`) = `r round(anova_site_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_site_p)`), indicating that the magnitude of the angle slope differed across sites. The angle slope `r ifelse(p_site_co < .05, "differed significantly", "did not differ significantly")` between mpieva-de and uniandes-co (β = `r round(beta_site_co, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_site_co, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_site_co)`), `r ifelse(p_site_ca < .05, "and was significantly shallower in western-ca than in mpieva-de", "but did not differ significantly between western-ca and mpieva-de")` (β = `r round(beta_site_ca, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_site_ca, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_site_ca)`). Age, operationalized as a three-level grouping, did not independently moderate the angle slope once site was accounted for (χ²(`r anova_age_df`) = `r round(anova_age_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_age_p)`).

For 2D stimuli, we observed a significant but smaller positive angle effect (β = `r round(beta_2d_main, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_2d_main, 2)`, t(`r round(df_2d_main, 1)`) = `r round(t_2d_main, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_2d_main)`). Adding site as a moderator `r ifelse(anova_2d_site_p < .05, "significantly improved model fit", "did not significantly improve model fit")` (χ²(`r anova_2d_site_df`) = `r round(anova_2d_site_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_2d_site_p)`), indicating that the angle slope `r ifelse(anova_2d_site_p < .05, "differed", "did not differ significantly")` across sites. The angle slope `r ifelse(p_2d_site_co < .05, "was significantly shallower", "did not differ significantly")` between uniandes-co and mpieva-de (β = `r round(beta_2d_site_co, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_2d_site_co, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_2d_site_co)`); did not differ significantly between western-ca and mpieva-de (β = `r round(beta_2d_site_ca, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_2d_site_ca, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_2d_site_ca)`); and `r ifelse(p_2d_site_co_wes < .05, "differed significantly", "did not differ significantly")` between uniandes-co and western-ca (β = `r round(beta_2d_site_co_wes, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_2d_site_co_wes, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_2d_site_co_wes)`). `r ifelse(all(c(p_2d_site_co, p_2d_site_ca, p_2d_site_co_wes) >= .05), "Although the omnibus test was significant, no individual pairwise comparison reached significance, suggesting the omnibus result reflects a joint pattern of site differences rather than any single site driving the effect.", "")`

@fig-rt-angle-per-run-no-cat plots mean reaction times (±95% confidence intervals) as a function of rotation angle, stratified by site and age group (binned for visualization; age was modeled continuously in all analyses), separately for 2D and 3D stimuli. Cell-level sample sizes underlying this figure are reported in [Appendix D (Sample Sizes)](#sec-apx-rt-angle-sample-sizes). Although the primary analyses modeled angle as a linear predictor over the 40–160° range, inspection of @fig-rt-angle-per-run-no-cat suggests some non-linearity in certain subgroups. The full 0–360° rotation functions — reported in [Appendix E (360° Angle Functions)](#sec-apx-360-angle) in the context of the strategy variation analysis — show the expected inverted-U, with RT increasing to a peak around 200–240° before declining symmetrically, consistent with participants taking the shortest rotational path. The 40–160° window analysed here captures the approximately linear rising limb of this function, supporting the use of a linear model for the angular disparity effect. Raw per-run data underlying these trends are reported in [Appendix D (Raw RT)](#sec-apx-irt-ability-age). Within-person dynamics — including trial-level variability and individual trajectories across runs are shown in [Appendix D (Within-Person Dynamics)](#sec-apx-within-person-dynamics).

```{r}
#| label: fig-rt-angle-per-run-no-cat
#| fig-cap: "**Reaction time by angle within age groups ±95% CI.** Note. Cells with fewer than 10 observations are excluded. Lines reflect descriptive means; statistical models were fit separately for 2D and 3D stimuli. Age groups shown for visualization only; age was modeled as a continuous predictor."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6.5

mrot_items_rt_runs <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  group_by(site, site_label, user_id, run_id, age, age_group,
           stimulus, item_group, angle) %>%
  summarise(
    rt_med = median(rt_s[correct == 1], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(item_group = str_to_upper(item_group))

mrot_items_rt_agebin_ci <- mrot_items_rt_runs %>%
  filter(!is.na(rt_med)) %>%
  group_by(site, site_label, stimulus, item_group, angle, age_group) %>%
  summarise(
    y   = mean(rt_med),
    sd  = sd(rt_med),
    n   = n(),
    se  = sd / sqrt(n),
    lwr = y - 1.96 * se,
    upr = y + 1.96 * se,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

min_n <- 10

.scale_colour_stimulus <- \(...) scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2", ...)

p_mrot_rt_angle_age_1 <- ggplot(
  mrot_items_rt_agebin_ci %>% filter(n >= min_n),
  aes(x = angle, y = y,
      group = interaction(item_group, stimulus),
      colour = stimulus, linetype = item_group)
) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), width = 2,
                linewidth = 0.35, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_grid(site_label ~ age_group) +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (°)", y = "Reaction time (s)",
       colour = "Stimulus", linetype = "Item type") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(40, 80, 120, 160)) +
  
  .scale_colour_stimulus() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p_mrot_rt_angle_age_1
```

## Analysis 3: Sex Differences 
Our third research question examined whether sex differences in mental rotation ability are detectable in this sample, and whether any such differences interact with age. We found that ability increased with age (β = `r round(lme4::fixef(sex_mod)["age"], 2)`, SE = `r round(coef(summary(sex_mod))["age","Std. Error"], 2)`, p < .001), with no evidence for a main effect of sex (β = `r round(lme4::fixef(sex_mod)["sexMale"], 2)`, p = `r format.pval(coef(summary(sex_mod))["sexMale","Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 2, eps = .001)`) or an age-by-sex interaction (β = `r round(lme4::fixef(sex_mod)["age:sexMale"], 2)`, p = `r format.pval(coef(summary(sex_mod))["age:sexMale","Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 2, eps = .001)`). The absence of sex differences is illustrated across all three sites in [Appendix C (Sex Differences)](#sec-apx-sex-diff-plot).

```{r}
#| label: strategy-analysis-prep
#| results: "hide"

# ability
ability_run <- mrot_df %>%
  group_by(site_label, user_id, run_id, age, age_group) %>%
  summarise(
    ability = mean(metric_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# prep trial-level data for the rich model
mrot_rich_data <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  # filter(!adaptive) %>% # note: added by Fionnuala, april 12
  mutate(
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(angle)),
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

# set sum-to-zero contrasts - by default, R uses treatment contrasts (Duck = reference). 
# This makes the "Angle" slope represent only Ducks (which is flat for everyone).
# Setting sum contrasts ensures the "Angle" slope represents the grand mean slope across all stimuli.
contrasts(mrot_rich_data$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_rich_data$stimulus))
m_rich <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_s * stimulus + trial_s +
    (1 + angle_s + trial_s | run_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mrot_rich_data,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 20000))
)

# extract subject-level random effects
ran_effs <- ranef(m_rich)$run_id %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("run_id") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(
    int_dev   = `(Intercept)`,
    slope_dev = angle_s,
    trial_dev = trial_s
  )

# fixed effects (global averages)
fix_int <- fixef(m_rich)["(Intercept)"]
fix_ang <- fixef(m_rich)["angle_s"]
fix_tri <- fixef(m_rich)["trial_s"]

# compute cognitive features (on log-RT scale)
rich_features_raw <- ran_effs %>%
  mutate(
    # Baseline Speed: Speed at angle 0 (Intercept)
    Baseline_Speed = fix_int + int_dev,
    # Absolute Slope: Time added per degree of rotation (Rotation Cost)
    Abs_Slope = fix_ang + slope_dev,
    # Relative Slope (Per Mike's suggestion)
    # "Is rotation expensive relative to their normal speed?"
    Rel_Slope = Abs_Slope / Baseline_Speed,
    # Learning Rate 
    Learning_Rate  = fix_tri + trial_dev
  )
# compute instability (Residual SD)
# We calculate SD of the *residuals* (not raw RT) to remove the "Task Difficulty" confound.
# This isolates internal inconsistency from the fact that some kids saw harder items.
mrot_rich_data$resid <- residuals(m_rich)

instability_data <- mrot_rich_data %>%
  group_by(run_id) %>%
  summarise(
    # Instability = SD of residuals (pure internal noise)
    Instability = sd(resid, na.rm = TRUE), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# join
rich_features_final <- rich_features_raw %>%
  left_join(instability_data, by = c("run_id")) %>% 
  left_join(ability_run,  by = c("run_id")) %>%
  mutate(Site = site_label) %>%
  # filter to ensure all needed features
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Baseline_Speed, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))
```

## Analysis 4: Strategy Variation
Our fourth research question asked, exploratorily, whether individual differences in children's RT profiles capture meaningful variation in strategy use, and whether strategy groupings differ across cultural contexts. We approach this as an attempt to characterize a continuum of engagement rather than identify discrete strategy types — from children who appear to disengage from the spatial structure of the task entirely, to those who engage effectively in varying ways. All analyses in this section are exploratory and descriptive; findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

To select the number of clusters, we evaluated solutions from k = 1–8 using the elbow method and average silhouette width; see [Appendix E (Cluster Validation)](#sec-apx-cluster) for full results. The statistically optimal solution was k = 2, but inspection of the resulting RT–angle functions revealed that this collapsed two theoretically distinguishable effective engagement profiles into a single region. We therefore adopted k = 3 on both empirical grounds (a moderate elbow inflection at k = 3) and theoretical grounds (the interpretability of the resulting RT profiles), treating the three profiles as descriptive anchors along a continuum rather than evidence for discrete strategy types.

The k = 3 solution identified three differentiable regions of the engagement continuum. Regions were labeled based on their trial-level RT patterns: children whose RT profiles showed no systematic angular sensitivity and high response instability were labeled *'Ineffective Strategies'*; those whose RT–angle functions peaked before declining at high disparities — consistent with exploiting reflective symmetry rather than full rotation — were labeled *'Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)'*; and those showing a monotonically increasing RT–angle function consistent with analog rotation were labeled *'Mental Rotation'*. Inspection of the RT–angle functions (@fig-rt-by-disparity) reveals meaningfully distinct patterns across the three groups.

The Ineffective Strategies group (n = `r ineff_n`, `r ineff_pct`%) is characterized by low ability (M = `r ineff_mean_ability`, SD = `r ineff_sd_ability`), the lowest absolute RT–angle slope of the three profiles (M = `r ineff_mean_abs_slope`), and high response instability (M = `r ineff_mean_instab`). Although this group's relative slope (M = `r ineff_mean_slope`) appears elevated relative to the two effective profiles, this reflects their faster baseline processing speed (M = `r ineff_mean_baseline`) rather than genuine angular sensitivity — dividing a small absolute slope by a fast baseline inflates the ratio without implying any rotation cost. The absence of angular sensitivity, 
combined with steeply declining accuracy (see [Appendix E (Accuracy-Angle Functions)](#sec-apx-accuracy-by-angle)),
represents a different pattern from simply being slow. The label 'Ineffective Strategies' captures a behaviorally heterogeneous group united by the absence of angular sensitivity rather than any shared approach to the task: children assigned here may include those who disengage entirely at higher angular disparities, those who rely on non-spatial heuristics such as position-based responding, and those who attempt rotation but abandon it before completion — the RT signature alone cannot distinguish between these possibilities.

The Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) group (n = `r flip_n`, `r flip_pct`%) is the second largest profile and shows the highest mean ability (M = `r flip_mean_ability`, SD = `r flip_sd_ability`). Their RT–angle function rises to a peak around 120° before declining at 160°; as items approach 180°, mirror images become easier to distinguish perceptually without requiring full rotation.

The Mental Rotation group (n = `r mrot_n`, `r mrot_pct`%) shows the classic monotonically increasing RT–angle function consistent with @shepard1971mental, with the steepest absolute slope (M = `r mrot_mean_abs_slope`, SD = `r mrot_sd_abs_slope`) and steepest relative slope (M = `r mrot_mean_slope`, SD = `r mrot_sd_slope`) among the two effective profiles. We note that flipping and feature matching are theoretically distinct processes [@mckee2025malleability; @hegarty2018ability], but are treated as a single profile here on pragmatic grounds that both tend to produce a weaker or less systematic angular disparity effect than analog rotation.

To validate the cluster solution against variables not used in its construction, we examined whether profiles differed in IRT-derived ability estimates. Ability differed across all pairwise comparisons (all *p*s < .0001; @fig-ability-boxplot), 
with the Ineffective Strategies group showing lower ability (M = `r ineff_mean_ability`, SD = `r ineff_sd_ability`) than both the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) (M = `r flip_mean_ability`, SD = `r flip_sd_ability`) and Mental Rotation (M = `r mrot_mean_ability`, SD = `r mrot_sd_ability`) groups. Interestingly, despite being the most common profile globally, the Mental Rotation group has lower mean ability than the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) group, even though it shows the RT signature the task was designed to elicit. This may reflect the greater cognitive cost of analog rotation relative to feature-matching strategies, particularly for the 2D stimuli where rotational demands are lower. Among the two effective profiles, relative RT slopes also differed significantly (p < .001; see [Appendix E (Relative RT Slope)](#sec-apx-slope-boxplot), with the Mental Rotation profile showing a steeper relative slope (M = `r mrot_mean_slope`) than the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profile (M = `r flip_mean_slope`), consistent with rotation cost scaling more strongly with angular disparity relative to baseline speed. Accuracy-angle functions by profile are reported in [Appendix E (Accuracy-Angle Functions)](#sec-apx-accuracy-by-angle) and corroborate the RT-based interpretation: the Ineffective Strategies group shows steeply declining accuracy with angle, while the two effective profiles maintain comparable accuracy throughout.

### Robustness checks {#sec-robustness-checks}
Three robustness checks are reported in full in the appendices. First, comparison of k=2 and k=3 solutions confirmed that k=2 collapsed two distinguishable RT–angle profiles into a single region, justifying the three-profile solution (see [Appendix E (Profile Summary Statistics)](#sec-apx-cluster-summary-stats) and [Appendix E (Cluster Validation)](#sec-apx-cluster)). Profile membership by age group is reported in [Appendix E (Strategy by Age)](#sec-apx-strategy-age-group). Second, dimensionality reduction via PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP consistently recovered the separation between the Ineffective Strategies group and the two effective engagement profiles, while the boundary between the Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profiles remained less clear — supporting the continuum interpretation see [Appendix E (Dimensionality Reduction)](#sec-apx-dimreduc). Third, re-analysis using full 0–360° rotation angles replicated the main findings and provided direct support for shortest-path rotation, with both the Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profiles showing near-symmetric inverted-U RT functions peaking around 200–240°, with the Mental Rotation profile showing the steeper rise consistent with the main analysis [Appendix E (360° Angle Functions)](#sec-apx-360-angle).
```{r}
#| label: local-clustering-agreement
#| include: false

cluster_vars <- c("Baseline_Speed", "Rel_Slope", "Abs_Slope", "Instability", "Learning_Rate")

stopifnot(all(cluster_vars %in% names(analysis_data)))
stopifnot(all(c("Site", "user_id", "run_id", "Strategy_Label") %in% names(analysis_data)))
stopifnot(nrow(analysis_data) == nrow(distinct(analysis_data, Site, user_id, run_id)))

# ARI function
ARI <- function(a, b) {
  a <- as.integer(factor(a))
  b <- as.integer(factor(b))
  tab <- table(a, b)
  n <- sum(tab)
  if (n <= 1) return(NA_real_)
  comb2    <- function(x) x * (x - 1) / 2
  sum_ij   <- sum(comb2(tab))
  sum_i    <- sum(comb2(rowSums(tab)))
  sum_j    <- sum(comb2(colSums(tab)))
  expected <- (sum_i * sum_j) / comb2(n)
  max_idx  <- 0.5 * (sum_i + sum_j)
  denom    <- max_idx - expected
  if (denom == 0) return(NA_real_)
  (sum_ij - expected) / denom
}

get_local_strategy_labels <- function(df_site,
                                      k = 3,
                                      seed = 123,
                                      nstart = 25,
                                      min_n = 30) {

  if (nrow(df_site) < min_n) return(NULL)
  set.seed(seed)

  X <- df_site %>%
    select(all_of(cluster_vars)) %>%
    scale() %>%
    as.matrix()

  km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = nstart)

  tmp <- df_site %>%
    mutate(Local_Cluster = factor(km$cluster))

  local_stats <- tmp %>%
    group_by(Local_Cluster) %>%
    summarise(
      mean_abil  = mean(ability,   na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_slope = mean(Rel_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(mean_abil)

  ineff_id     <- local_stats %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Local_Cluster) %>% as.character()
  other_two    <- local_stats %>% filter(as.character(Local_Cluster) != ineff_id) %>% arrange(mean_slope)
  other_eff_id <- other_two   %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Local_Cluster) %>% as.character()
  mrot_id      <- other_two   %>% slice(2) %>% pull(Local_Cluster) %>% as.character()

  tmp %>%
    mutate(
      Strategy_Local = case_when(
        as.character(Local_Cluster) == ineff_id ~ "Ineffective Strategies",
        as.character(Local_Cluster) == other_eff_id ~ "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)",
        as.character(Local_Cluster) == mrot_id ~ "Mental Rotation"
      ),
      Strategy_Local = factor(Strategy_Local, levels = levels(analysis_data$Strategy_Label))
    ) %>%
    select(Site, user_id, Strategy_Local)
}

# fit local models independently within each site
local_labels_all <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(Site) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  purrr::map_dfr(get_local_strategy_labels)

analysis_local <- analysis_data %>%
  select(-any_of("Strategy_Local")) %>%
  left_join(local_labels_all, by = c("Site", "user_id"))

# agreement (3-class)
agreement_3class <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  group_by(Site) %>%
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    pct_agree = mean(Strategy_Local == Strategy_Label),
    ARI       = ARI(Strategy_Label, Strategy_Local),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

agreement_3class

# confusion matrices per site — save split first to avoid pipe . scoping issue
site_splits <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  group_split(Site)

confusion_by_site <- site_splits %>%
  purrr::set_names(purrr::map_chr(site_splits, ~ unique(.x$Site))) %>%
  purrr::map(~ table(.x$Strategy_Local, .x$Strategy_Label))

confusion_by_site

# recall + purity
recall_tbl <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  count(Site, Strategy_Label, Strategy_Local) %>%
  group_by(Site, Strategy_Label) %>%
  mutate(recall = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

purity_tbl <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  count(Site, Strategy_Local, Strategy_Label) %>%
  group_by(Site, Strategy_Local) %>%
  mutate(purity = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

diag_summary <- recall_tbl %>%
  filter(Strategy_Label == Strategy_Local) %>%
  transmute(Site, Strategy = Strategy_Label, recall) %>%
  left_join(
    purity_tbl %>%
      filter(Strategy_Local == Strategy_Label) %>%
      transmute(Site, Strategy = Strategy_Local, purity),
    by = c("Site", "Strategy")
  )

diag_summary
```

```{r}
get_diag <- function(site, label) {
  out <- diag_summary[diag_summary$Site == site & diag_summary$Strategy == label, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(out) == 0) {
    return(data.frame(Site = site, Strategy = label, recall = NA_real_, purity = NA_real_))
  }
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1)
  out
}

# off-diagonal moves
get_move <- function(tab, local_lab, global_lab) {
  stopifnot(local_lab %in% rownames(tab), global_lab %in% colnames(tab))
  n     <- tab[local_lab, global_lab]
  denom <- sum(tab[, global_lab])
  list(n = as.numeric(n), denom = as.numeric(denom), prop = as.numeric(n) / as.numeric(denom))
}
```

### Cross-Cultural Consistency of Strategy Profiles
We next examined whether the continuum structure is recoverable within each site independently by re-running the k-means procedure separately within each site and computing agreement between the local and global profile assignments for each participant, using percent agreement (the proportion of participants assigned to the same profile by both solutions) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), alongside per-profile recall and purity.

Uniandes-co showed the strongest overall recovery (percent agreement = `r uni_pct_agree`, ARI = `r uni_ari`), with high recall and purity across all three profiles — including the Mental Rotation profile (recall = `r uni_mrot_recall`, purity = `r uni_mrot_purity`). This suggests the full continuum structure is locally recoverable when sample sizes are adequate and testing conditions are consistent.

Mpieva-de showed moderate overall agreement (`r mpi_pct_agree`, ARI = `r mpi_ari`), driven primarily by poor recovery of the Ineffective Strategies profile locally (recall = `r mpi_ineff_recall`). Notably, the Mental Rotation profile was well-recovered in mpieva-de (recall = `r mpi_mrot_recall`, purity = `r mpi_mrot_purity`), suggesting the finer subdivision within the effective end of the continuum is detectable there. The lower overall agreement at mpieva-de may reflect the greater RT variability introduced by its remote, home-based testing format.

Western-ca showed the lowest overall agreement (`r wes_pct_agree`, ARI = `r wes_ari`), but for a qualitatively different reason. The local solution assigned the large majority of children to a single group that mapped onto the global Mental Rotation profile — producing near-perfect recall for that profile (`r wes_mrot_recall`) but low purity (`r wes_mrot_purity`), and near-zero recall for both the Ineffective Strategies (`r wes_ineff_recall`) and Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) (`r wes_flip_recall`) profiles. This pattern suggests the local solution in western-ca collapsed the full continuum into a single dominant region rather than failing to recover any particular profile. The smaller sample size at western-ca likely contributed to this instability.

# Discussion
The central aim of this study was to establish whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task measures the same underlying construct across three culturally diverse sites. The answer, across four distinct levels of analysis, is largely yes. The task achieves scalar measurement invariance — including across a low-to-middle-income site from the Global South — indicating that both the ordering and spacing of items on the latent scale are consistent across cultural contexts [@putnick2016measurement]. The angular disparity effect replicates robustly for 3D stimuli across all three sites, and is present though attenuated for 2D stimuli, providing process-level evidence that performance is driven by the spatial demands of the task in the way theory predicts [@shepard1971mental] — a form of evidence that is distinct from, and complementary to, the psychometric result. The absence of a main effect of sex or any age-by-sex interaction is consistent with the meta-analytic picture for child-friendly tasks in this age range [@lauer2019development], and its replication across all three international sites extends prior null findings beyond the Western convenience samples in which they have predominantly been documented [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. And at the level of individual behavioral profiles, the broad distinction between children who disengage from the task's spatial demands and those who engage effectively is recoverable within each site independently, even if the finer subdivision between engagement types shows more variable local recovery. That these convergent forms of evidence emerge across geographically and culturally diverse samples supports the interpretation that the task is capturing individual differences in a common/universal spatial reasoning construct rather than one that is specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was developed [@davis2021cultural; @henrich2010weirdest].

## Cross-Site Invariance
Turning to our first research question, the demonstration of scalar invariance under a 2PL model establishes that the mental rotation task functions comparably across pilot sites — that items are ordered by difficulty and discrimination in the same way for children in Bogotá as for children in Leipzig or London, Ontario, and that ability estimates can be placed on a common latent scale [@putnick2016measurement]. This is a meaningful result: tasks developed in one context do not automatically achieve psychometric equivalence when administered elsewhere [@van2004bias], and the inclusion of a low-to-middle-income site from the Global South makes this a stronger test than studies conducted entirely within high-income North American and European samples. That said, scalar invariance establishes metric comparability rather than cultural equivalence in any deeper sense. With only one non-Western site — though one spanning both urban and rural schools, representing a meaningfully different cultural and socioeconomic context from the German and Canadian samples — the present findings should be treated as an encouraging foundation rather than evidence of broad cross-cultural portability. Further validation across more culturally and socioeconomically diverse sites will be needed before stronger claims can be made. The LEVANTE project is expanding to include additional sites in low- and middle-income countries in coming years, which will provide the opportunity to subject these findings to a more demanding cross-cultural test. Finally, given that LEVANTE sites differ substantially in sampling, recruitment, and testing format, site level performance differences are not interpreted here regardless of the invariance results; however, we believe the consistency of patterns within and across sites remains informative.

## Angular Sensitivity
Our second research question asked whether performance is driven by the spatial properties of the stimuli. The key benchmark here is the angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental: as the rotational distance between a 3D target and its match increases, so too does the time required to judge whether they correspond. This relationship, among the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology [@cooper1973chronometric; @peters2008applications], has been demonstrated extensively in children and adults from middle-to-high-income Western convenience samples [@kaltner2016developmental; @jansen2015role], but had not previously been established in culturally diverse samples of children. Its consistent emergence here, across all three sites, suggests that the underlying cognitive process it indexes — the spatially continuous transformation of object orientation — is not specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was originally documented. This matters because psychometric equivalence and process-level validity are distinct forms of evidence. It is one thing to show that a task achieves comparable difficulty ordering across sites; it is another to show that performance is sensitive to the spatial structure of the stimuli in the way that mental rotation theory predicts [@borsboom2004concept]. The angular disparity effect provides the latter, and its cross-cultural replication substantially strengthens the case that the task is engaging spatial cognition specifically, rather than some culturally-variable combination of task-general skills. The shallower slope for 2D stimuli likely reflects the greater familiarity of duck and rabbit silhouettes relative to the 3D geometric shapes: when stimuli are easy to tell apart, children can make same/different judgments by comparing surface features rather than rotating, producing a weaker RT–angle relationship [@folk1987effects; @bethell1988mental].

Children at mpieva-de showed both higher baseline response times and steeper absolute RT–angle slopes than the other two sites — a pattern consistent with a testing format explanation rather than a genuine cultural difference in angular sensitivity. Remote home-based testing on family devices, as used at mpieva-de, may introduce environmental variability that is likely to inflate both baseline RT and trial-to-trial noise; because absolute slopes scale with baseline speed, this would mechanically produce steeper slopes even without greater rotation sensitivity, a pattern visible in the wider raw RT distributions at mpieva-de (@sec-apx-irt-ability-age). 

## Sex Differences
Our third research question asked whether sex differences in mental rotation ability are detectable in this sample, and whether any such differences interact with age. The absence of a main effect of sex or an age-by-sex interaction replicates the pattern reported in several recent studies of primary school-aged children using child-friendly mental rotation tasks [@hodgkiss2021developmental; @lauer2019development], and is consistent with the meta-analytic picture: reliable sex differences in mental rotation are small and inconsistent in this age range, particularly for tasks using 2D stimuli and child-friendly formats of the kind used here [@lauer2019development]. The LEVANTE task's design — 2D animal silhouettes alongside 3D block figures — places it squarely in the category of tasks where the meta-analytic expectation for a gender difference is modest at best. Notably, the null finding held across all three international study sites, extending prior null results beyond the middle-to-high-income Western samples in which they have predominantly been documented [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. Taken together, the sex difference results are consistent with the broader argument of this paper: that the task captures a spatially-driven construct that is consistent across cultural contexts.

## Strategy Variation
Our fourth research question asked, exploratorily, whether trial-level RT patterns capture meaningful variation in strategy use, and whether the distribution of strategies differs across sites. Research with adults has established that solvers draw on a range of strategies when performing mental rotation tasks, spanning a holistic-analytic continuum [@gluck2003spatial], and that strategy selection varies across individuals and shifts with task demands [@nazareth2019strategy]. Crucially, such strategies can be identified from patterns in RT data even in the absence of direct observation [@geiser2006separating], providing the methodological basis for the present analysis — though we treat the resulting profiles as descriptive anchors along a continuum of engagement rather than as evidence for discrete strategy types.
