The two effective profiles — Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) and Mental Rotation — are distinguished primarily by the shape of their RT–angle functions, but not by accuracy, which was higher for the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) group. Importantly, the two profile-defining dimensions do different separating work: ability distinguishes the Ineffective Strategies group from both effective profiles, while relative RT slope distinguishes the two effective profiles from each other — and it is this complementary structure that justifies retaining three profiles rather than two. An interesting finding is that the Mental Rotation profile is both the most common globally (n = `r mrot_n`, `r mrot_pct`%) and yet associated with lower mean ability than the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) group — the reverse of what the broader literature might lead us to expect [@khooshabeh2013individual; @heil2008sex], though the effect is modest and the groups overlap considerably in ability. This could suggest that RT signatures consistent with full analog rotation carry a greater cognitive cost than feature-based engagement [@just1985cognitive; @khooshabeh2013individual], particularly for the 2D stimuli where rotational demands are lower. The overlap between these two profiles in the behavioral feature space — consistent across all three dimensionality reduction methods [Appendix E (Dimensionality Reduction)](#sec-apx-dimreduc) — reinforces this picture: the distinction between them is gradient rather than categorical. 

The recoverability of this continuum structure varies across sites in qualitatively different ways: uniandes-co recovered all three regions well, mpieva-de recovered the effective subdivision but showed poor recovery of the Ineffective Strategies profile — possibly reflecting the greater RT variability introduced by its remote, home-based testing format — and western-ca collapsed the full continuum into a single dominant region, likely reflecting its smaller sample size (n = \r wes_n`)` rather than a genuine absence of strategy variation. We retain the three-profile distinction in the global solution because collapsing to k=2 obscures a theoretically meaningful difference in RT–angle profile shape, but treat it as a convenient descriptive marker rather than evidence for discrete strategy types. Taken together, the exploratory clustering exercise reveals a meaningful continuum of engagement — from children who appear to disengage from the task's spatial elements entirely, to those who solve it effectively through different spatial processes — but larger, more methodologically consistent samples will be needed before firm conclusions about cross-cultural variation in strategy profiles can be drawn.

Read alongside the measurement invariance result, these findings raise an apparent paradox — but it is resolvable. Scalar invariance establishes that between-person differences in ability are organised comparably across sites; the clustering analysis establishes that within-person processing varies. These are compatible: children can arrive at commensurable ability estimates via different cognitive routes. The invariance result does not imply a single shared cognitive process — only that whatever processes children bring to the task, the resulting ability differences are structured the same way across cultural contexts.

## Limitations
Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. Although the three sites span different continents and linguistic contexts, two of the three are middle-to-high-income Western samples, and while the Colombian site is more socioeconomically diverse — spanning urban schools in Bogotá and rural schools in surrounding departments — the sample as a whole remains far from representative of the full range of cultural environments in which children develop. The LEVANTE project has already expanded to six additional sites since this initial data collection, with future efforts prioritizing data collection in low- and middle-income countries, which will substantially broaden the cultural scope of findings like those reported here. Sample sizes were also unbalanced across sites, with the Canadian sample smaller overall, which limits the precision of site-level estimates and the power to detect cross-site differences. The cross-sectional design is a further constraint: developmental trajectories here are inferred from age differences between children rather than observed directly. Longitudinal data are currently being collected and processed, however, and will allow this question to be addressed more directly in due course. Finally, the strategy clustering analysis is exploratory and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The profiles are inferred from behavioral proxies rather than directly observed strategies, and replication in larger, more diverse, and more methodologically consistent samples will be needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.

# Conclusion
Four research questions motivated this study, each asking in a different way whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task is doing consistent and interpretable work across culturally diverse settings. Across all four, the answer is largely affirmative. Scalar measurement invariance holds across sites including a low-to-middle-income site from the Global South; the angular disparity effect replicates as a process-level signature of spatial engagement; sex differences are absent in a pattern consistent with the meta-analytic picture for this age range and task type; and a meaningful continuum of engagement strategies is detectable, at least in broad outline, across all three sites. These findings do not mean that mental rotation development is uniform across children or contexts — the substantial individual variability within sites, and the tentative evidence for cross-cultural differences in strategy distributions, suggest there is much still to understand about what drives variation in spatial ability across children. But they do mean that the task is measuring something consistent — that when a child in Bogotá, a child in Leipzig, and a child in London (Ontario) sit down to judge whether two rotated objects are the same, they are, by and large, engaging the same cognitive process. Such consistency is the foundation on which meaningful cross-cultural comparisons can be built.

```{r}
    aes(x = angle, y = y, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr,
        colour = stimulus, linetype = item_group,
        group = interaction(item_group, stimulus)),
    width = 2,
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = mrot_items_rt_agebin_ci,
    aes(x = angle, y = y,
        colour = stimulus,
        group = interaction(item_group, stimulus)),

  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = mrot_items_rt_agebin_ci,
    aes(x = angle, y = y,
        colour = stimulus, linetype = item_group,
        group = interaction(item_group, stimulus)),
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  facet_grid(site_label ~ age_group) +
  .scale_colour_stimulus() +
  labs(
    #title = "Mental Rotation: RT by angle within age groups ±95% CI",
    x = "Rotation angle (°)",

p_mrot_rt_angle_age_2
```

## Within-Person Dynamics {#sec-apx-within-person-dynamics}
Having established that 3D stimuli elicit a clear angular disparity effect while 2D stimuli do to a lesser extent, we next asked a complementary question: whether children show sensitivity to task demands as they unfold in real time — specifically, whether reaction times shift systematically at the transition from 2D to 3D stimuli, and whether practice effects are detectable within blocks. To isolate time-on-task effects from item-driven RT changes, we residualized log-RTs on angle, stimulus, and item type prior to analysis.
```{r}
#| label: fig-within-person-trials
#| fig-cap: "**Trial-level reaction time dynamics (angle-residualised).** Mean residual log-RT across trials for each non-adaptive site ±SE. The dashed line marks the 2D→3D transition. Retest and CAT data removed."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

# prep: remove CAT data
trial_resid_data <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  filter(!adaptive, correct == 1)

# residualize log_rt on angle + stimulus + item_group
resid_model <- lm(log_rt ~ angle + stimulus + item_group, 
                  data = trial_resid_data)

trial_resid_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  mutate(log_rt_resid = residuals(resid_model),
         block = item_group |> str_to_upper())

transition_trial <- trial_resid_data |>
  filter(item_group == "3d") |>
  pull(trial_number) |>
  min()

# plot
ggplot(trial_resid_data, 
       aes(x = trial_number, y = log_rt_resid, 
           color = site_label, fill = site_label)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = interaction(site_label, block)),
              method = "loess", span = 0.75, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = transition_trial - 0.5, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "lightgrey", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = transition_trial + 1, y = Inf,
           label = "Start of 3D block", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  labs(
    x     = "Trial number",
    y     = "Residual reaction time",
    color = "Site",
    fill  = "Site"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: within-person-models
#| include: false

# center trial number within each block so the intercept at transition is interpretable
within_person_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  mutate(
    block         = factor(block, levels = c("2D", "3D")),
    # trial number centered within block
    trial_c       = trial_number - transition_trial,
    site          = factor(site)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(trial_number), !is.na(log_rt_resid))

# Model 1: continuous trial slope only 
m_wp_continuous <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 2: add block as main effect — tests for discontinuous jump at transition
m_wp_jump <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + block + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 3: add trial × block interaction — tests whether slope changes after transition
m_wp_slope <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c * block + (1 + trial_c | run_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# model comparisons
anova_wp_jump  <- anova(m_wp_continuous, m_wp_jump)   # is there a jump?
anova_wp_slope <- anova(m_wp_jump, m_wp_slope)  

# extract key numbers
wp_coefs       <- coef(summary(m_wp_slope))

# block jump (intercept shift at transition)
beta_wp_block  <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_block    <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_block     <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# within-block trial slope (2D block)
beta_wp_trial  <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Estimate"]
se_wp_trial    <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_trial     <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# interaction: does slope differ in 3D block?
beta_wp_int    <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_int      <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_int       <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# anova numbers for inline reporting
wp_jump_chisq  <- anova_wp_jump$Chisq[2]
wp_jump_df     <- anova_wp_jump$Df[2]
wp_jump_p      <- anova_wp_jump[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]

wp_slope_chisq <- anova_wp_slope$Chisq[2]
wp_slope_df    <- anova_wp_slope$Df[2]
wp_slope_p     <- anova_wp_slope[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]
```
\clearpage

@fig-within-person-trials plots mean residual log-RT across trials for each site. To test for a discontinuous shift in RT at the 2D→3D block transition and for within-block practice effects, we fitted a series of mixed-effects models predicting residual log-RT from trial number, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes.

First, a model including a block indicator (2D vs 3D) significantly improved fit over a continuous trial-slope model (χ²(`r wp_jump_df`) = `r round(wp_jump_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_jump_p)`), confirming that the increase in RT at the 2D→3D transition is discontinuous rather than a continuation of a gradual trend. The block coefficient indicates a sudden upward shift in residual RT at trial 48 (β = `r round(beta_wp_block, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_block, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_block)`), consistent with children recalibrating their processing demands at the block boundary rather than adapting incrementally.

Second, within each block, RTs decreased across trials, indicating a practice effect operating independently of angular disparity (β = `r round(beta_wp_trial, 4)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_trial, 4)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_trial)`). Adding a trial × block interaction `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, "significantly improved model fit", "did not significantly improve model fit")` (χ²(`r wp_slope_df`) = `r round(wp_slope_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_slope_p)`) `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, paste0(", with the within-block acceleration differing between the 2D and 3D blocks (β = ", round(beta_wp_int, 3), ", SE = ", round(se_wp_int, 3), ", p ", fmt_p(p_wp_int), ")"), "")`. Both patterns — the discontinuous block transition and the within-block acceleration — were qualitatively consistent across all three sites, further extending the cross-cultural consistency observed in the angular disparity analysis.

## Profile Summary Statistics {#sec-apx-cluster-summary-stats}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-cluster-summary
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| tbl-cap: "**Profile summary statistics**. The Mental Rotation profile shows the steepest absolute RT–angle slope but lower mean ability than the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profile. The Ineffective Strategies profile is characterized by near-zero slope and high response instability rather than slow or fast processing per se. Note that the Ineffective Strategies profile's elevated relative slope reflects a fast baseline speed rather than genuine angular sensitivity — its absolute slope is the lowest of the three profiles."

analysis_data %>%
  group_by(Strategy_Label) %>%
  summarise(
    n              = n(),
    mean_ability   = mean(ability, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_ability     = sd(ability, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_rel_slope = mean(Rel_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_rel_slope   = sd(Rel_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_abs_slope = mean(Abs_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_abs_slope   = sd(Abs_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_rel_slope)) %>%
  transmute(
    Strategy       = Strategy_Label,
    N              = n,
    `Mean Ability` = mean_ability,
    `SD Ability`   = sd_ability,
    `Mean Rel. Slope` = mean_rel_slope,
    `SD Rel. Slope`   = sd_rel_slope,
    `Mean Abs. Slope` = mean_abs_slope,
    `SD Abs. Slope`   = sd_abs_slope
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = md("")) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(`Mean Ability`, `SD Ability`, 
                `Mean Rel. Slope`, `SD Rel. Slope`,
                `Mean Abs. Slope`, `SD Abs. Slope`),
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = N, decimals = 0, use_seps = FALSE) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(Strategy, N)) %>%
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = where(is.numeric)) %>%
  cols_width(
    Strategy ~ px(160),
    N        ~ px(40),
    everything() ~ px(65)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(label = "Ability",         columns = c(`Mean Ability`, `SD Ability`)) %>%
  tab_spanner(label = "Relative Slope",  columns = c(`Mean Rel. Slope`, `SD Rel. Slope`)) %>%
  tab_spanner(label = "Absolute Slope",  columns = c(`Mean Abs. Slope`, `SD Abs. Slope`)) %>%
  cols_label_with(fn = \(x) str_extract(x, "^[A-z]+")) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    data_row.padding = px(3)
  )
```
## Cluster Solution Validation {#sec-apx-cluster}
To assess the appropriateness of the three-profile solution, we evaluated cluster quality across k = 1–8 using two complementary metrics: total within-cluster sum of squares (the elbow method) and average silhouette width (@fig-k-sweep-validation). The silhouette analysis identified k = 2 as the statistically optimal solution, with average silhouette width peaking at 0.35 before declining steeply at k = 3 and remaining low thereafter. The elbow plot showed a moderate inflection at k = 3, after which additional clusters yielded diminishing reductions in within-cluster variance. To examine whether k = 2 was substantively adequate, we examined the RT–angle functions of the resulting two-cluster solution (@fig-k2-cluster-check). The higher-ability cluster displayed a characteristic inverted-U RT function, rising to a peak around 120° before declining at 160° — a pattern that, in the three-cluster solution, distinguishes the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) and Mental Rotation groups. This indicates that k = 2 collapses two distinguishable effective engagement profiles into a single region, obscuring a theoretically meaningful behavioral difference. We therefore adopted k = 3 on both empirical grounds (the elbow inflection) and theoretical grounds (the interpretability of the resulting RT profiles), noting that the three profiles are treated as convenient descriptive anchors along a continuum rather than evidence for discrete strategy types.

```{r}
#| label: fig-k-sweep-validation
#| eval: true
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "**Cluster validation metrics: Elbow Method (left) and Silhouette Analysis (right).** The elbow plot shows a bend at k=3, and silhouette width peaks at k=2 before declining, providing partial support for the 3-cluster solution."

.theme <- theme_get()
p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8, linecolor = pal$grey) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = 2, color = pal$grey) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters k") +
  .theme

p_sil <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8, linecolor = pal$grey) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters k") +
  .theme

grid.arrange(p_elbow, p_sil, nrow = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-k2-cluster-check
#| eval: true
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**RT–angle functions for the k=2 solution.** The higher-ability cluster displays an inverted-U RT curve consistent with a mix of Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) engagement profiles, suggesting that k=2 collapses two distinguishable effective profiles into a single region."

# Set up Input (same features as main analysis)
analysis_data_k2 <- rich_features_final %>%
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Baseline_Speed, Abs_Slope, Rel_Slope, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

global_input_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 %>%
  select(Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Instability, Abs_Slope, Learning_Rate) %>%
  scale()

# Run K-Means with K=2 
set.seed(123)
k_global_2 <- kmeans(global_input_k2, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
analysis_data_k2$Global_Cluster <- as.factor(k_global_2$cluster)

# Label the 2 Clusters 
# We define them simply by Ability (Low vs High) since we can't split by slope yet
cluster_stats_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 %>%
  group_by(Global_Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_ability = mean(ability), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Identify Lower Ability Cluster
low_eff_id <- cluster_stats_k2 %>% arrange(mean_ability) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)
# The other one is High Efficiency
high_eff_id <- cluster_stats_k2 %>% arrange(desc(mean_ability)) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)

analysis_data_k2 <- analysis_data_k2 %>%
  mutate(Strategy_Label = case_when(
    Global_Cluster == low_eff_id ~ "Low Efficiency (Cluster 1)",
    Global_Cluster == high_eff_id ~ "High Efficiency (Cluster 2)"
  ))

k2_colors <- c(
  "Low Efficiency (Cluster 1)"  = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[1],
  "High Efficiency (Cluster 2)" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[2]
)

# Plot the Curves (Visual Check)
# Join labels to raw data
rt_by_strategy_k2 <- mrot_rich_data %>%
  left_join(
    analysis_data_k2 %>% select(run_id, Strategy_Label),
    by = c("run_id")
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Label), is.finite(log_rt), is.finite(angle))

# Calculate User Means
rt_user_angle_k2 <- rt_by_strategy_k2 %>%
  group_by(Strategy_Label, run_id, angle) %>%
  summarise(user_mean_log_rt = mean(log_rt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Calculate Group Means
rt_summary_k2 <- rt_user_angle_k2 %>%
  group_by(Strategy_Label, angle) %>%
  summarise(
    n_users     = n_distinct(run_id),
    mean_log_rt = mean(user_mean_log_rt, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_log_rt   = sd(user_mean_log_rt, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_users),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# plot
ggplot(rt_summary_k2, aes(x = angle, y = mean_log_rt, colour = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_log_rt - 1.96*se_log_rt, 
                  ymax = mean_log_rt + 1.96*se_log_rt, 
                  fill = Strategy_Label), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = k2_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = k2_colors) +
  labs(
    title    = NULL,
    subtitle = NULL,
    y = "Mean log reaction time (s)",
    # y = "Mean log(RT) (participant-weighted)", 
    x = "Rotation angle (°)",
    colour = "Strategy", fill = "Strategy"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Strategy Use Across Age Groups {#sec-apx-strategy-age-group}
```{r}
#| label: strategy-age-data
#| include: false

strategy_by_age <- analysis_data |>
  count(age_group, Strategy_Label) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  mutate(prop = round(n / sum(n), 2)) |>
  ungroup()

get_prop <- function(age_grp, strategy) {
  strategy_by_age[
    strategy_by_age$age_group == age_grp & 
    strategy_by_age$Strategy_Label == strategy, 
    "prop"
  ][[1]]
}

# pre-computed scalars for inline R
ineff_pct_young <- get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100
ineff_pct_mid   <- get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100
ineff_pct_old   <- get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100
flip_pct_young  <- get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)") * 100
flip_pct_mid    <- get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)") * 100
flip_pct_old    <- get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)") * 100
mrot_pct_young  <- get_prop("[5,8.3]", "Mental Rotation") * 100
mrot_pct_mid    <- get_prop("(8.3,10.6]", "Mental Rotation") * 100
mrot_pct_old    <- get_prop("(10.6,13.7]", "Mental Rotation") * 100
```
We examined whether the distribution of engagement profiles varied across age groups (@fig-strategy-by-age). This analysis is purely descriptive — formal inferential testing would be circular given that both the age groupings and profile assignments are derived from the data, and the profile solution itself carries the caveats described above. With those caveats in mind, a descriptive pattern is nonetheless visible. The proportion of children assigned to the Ineffective Strategies profile declined substantially with age, from `r ineff_pct_young`% in the youngest group (ages 5–8.3) to `r ineff_pct_mid`% (ages 8.3–10.6) and `r ineff_pct_old`% (ages 10.6–13.7). This was accompanied by a corresponding increase in the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profile, from `r flip_pct_young`% to `r flip_pct_mid`% and `r flip_pct_old`%. By contrast, the proportion assigned to the Mental Rotation profile remained consistent across age groups (`r mrot_pct_young`%, `r mrot_pct_mid`%, `r mrot_pct_old`%). The primary developmental shift thus appears to be a move away from task disengagement toward effective feature-matching engagement profiles, with the proportion showing analog rotation signatures remaining comparatively stable across this age range.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strategy-by-age
#| fig-align: "center"
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "**Strategy profile proportions by age group.**"

strategy_by_age %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = prop, fill = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = my_colors,
                    labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, width = 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion()) +
  labs(x = "Age group (years)",
       y = "Proportion in strategy profile",
       fill = "Strategy") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Dimensionality Reduction Checks {#sec-apx-dimreduc}
To validate the continuum structure, we examined whether the three-profile solution was recoverable using alternative dimensionality reduction methods: PCA (@fig-pca-check), t-SNE (@fig-tsne-check), and UMAP (@fig-umap-check). PCA loadings were also inspected to characterize the underlying feature structure (@fig-pca-loadings).

Results were consistent across all three methods in one key respect: the Ineffective Strategies group was clearly and reliably separated from the two effective engagement profiles, appearing as a distinct region in all three projections — the right end of PC1 in the PCA, and distinct regions in the t-SNE and UMAP projections. This convergent separation provides strong evidence that this group occupies a genuinely distinct region of the feature space. The boundary between the Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profiles was, however, substantially less clear. Green and blue points overlapped considerably across all three visualizations, suggesting these two profiles represent adjacent regions of a continuum rather than fully discrete groupings — a finding consistent with the silhouette analysis favoring k = 2.

Inspection of the PCA loadings offered interpretive support for the feature set. PC1 loaded positively on Instability and Relative Slope, and negatively on Baseline Speed, Absolute Slope, and Learning Rate, reflecting a dimension that contrasts inefficient, variable engagement (high instability, elevated relative slope, slow baseline) with efficient, consistent processing (fast baseline, steeper absolute slope, stronger learning across trials). This dimension primarily separates the Ineffective Strategies group from the two effective profiles. PC2 loaded most strongly on Relative Slope and Absolute Slope — both positive — with Learning Rate loading negatively, reflecting a rotation cost dimension that captures angular sensitivity largely independent of general processing speed. This dimension provides the primary separation between the two effective profiles. The fact that these two components map onto theoretically meaningful and distinct dimensions provides confidence that the clustering features are not redundant.

## Full 0–360° Angle Functions check {#sec-apx-360-angle}
The primary analyses modeled angular disparity as the shortest path to upright, capped at 180°, on the assumption that participants take the most efficient route when rotating stimuli. To test this assumption, we re-ran the clustering using full 0–360° rotation angles and plotted RT and accuracy functions across the complete angular range (@fig-rt-angle-by-strategy-360, @fig-accuracy-angle-by-strategy-360). We verified that the angular disparity variable was correctly computed, confirming that full rotation angles were accurately recoded to their shortest-path equivalents (e.g., a 320° rotation has a disparity of 40°). The 360° clustering produced identical profile assignments to the main analysis (Ineffective Strategies: n = 228; Mental Rotation: n = 511; Other Effective Strategies: n = 419), confirming that the robustness check is examining the same profiles under a different angle representation.

The results were broadly consistent with the disparity-based analyses and provided direct support for the shortest-path assumption. Both the Mental Rotation and Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profiles showed RT functions that increased from 40° to a peak around 200–240°, then declined as angles approached 320°, forming the expected near-symmetric inverted-U around 180°. This pattern is what would be predicted if participants always rotate via the shorter available path, and would not be expected under a fixed-direction rotation strategy.

The Mental Rotation profile showed the steeper and higher RT function throughout, rising from a mean log RT of 1.02 at 40° to a peak of 1.85 at 240° before declining to 1.49 at 320°. The Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profile rose more gradually, peaking at 1.46 at 240° — consistent with less angular sensitivity relative to baseline speed, as reflected in its shallower relative slope in the main analysis. Notably, the inverted-U shape of the Other Effective profile in the full 360° data is more symmetric than the 120° peak-and-decline pattern observed in the disparity-capped data, suggesting the apparent flipping signature in the main analysis may partly reflect the capping of angles at 180° rather than a pure reflective symmetry strategy. Accuracy for both effective profiles showed a corresponding U-shaped function, declining to a minimum around 160–200° before recovering at higher angles, with the Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping) profile maintaining the highest accuracy throughout. The Ineffective Strategies profile again showed a broadly flat and declining RT function across the full angular range, with accuracy remaining low at peak angles and showing only a modest recovery above 240°, further supporting the interpretation that these children are not engaging with the spatial structure of the items.
```{r}
#| label: robustness-check-all-angles
#| results: "hide"

# NOTE: all objects in this and subsequent 360° chunks use _360 suffixes to avoid overwriting main analysis objects. These chunks must remain the
# last substantive analysis chunks in the document.

mrot_rich_data_360 <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  rename(ang_disparity = angle,
         angle = angle_full) %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(ang_disparity)),
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

contrasts(mrot_rich_data_360$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_rich_data_360$stimulus))

m_rich_360 <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_s * stimulus + trial_s +
    (1 + angle_s + trial_s | run_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mrot_rich_data_360,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 20000))
)

ran_effs_360 <- ranef(m_rich_360)$run_id %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("run_id") %>%
  rename(
    int_dev   = `(Intercept)`,
    slope_dev = angle_s,
    trial_dev = trial_s
  )

fix_int_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["(Intercept)"]
fix_ang_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["angle_s"]
fix_tri_360 <- fixef(m_rich_360)["trial_s"]

rich_features_raw_360 <- ran_effs_360 %>%
  mutate(
    Baseline_Speed = fix_int_360 + int_dev,
    Abs_Slope      = fix_ang_360 + slope_dev,
    Rel_Slope      = Abs_Slope / Baseline_Speed,
    Learning_Rate  = fix_tri_360 + trial_dev
  )

mrot_rich_data_360$resid <- residuals(m_rich_360)

instability_data_360 <- mrot_rich_data_360 %>%
  group_by(run_id) %>%
  summarise(
    Instability = sd(resid, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

rich_features_final_360 <- rich_features_raw_360 %>%
  left_join(instability_data_360, by = "run_id") %>%
  left_join(ability_run, by = "run_id") %>%
  mutate(Site = site_label) %>%
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Baseline_Speed, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))

# Check: ang_disparity should never exceed 180
summary(mrot_rich_data_360$ang_disparity)

# Spot check a few items
mrot_rich_data_360 %>%
  select(item, item_original, angle, ang_disparity) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  arrange(item_original) %>%
  head(20)
  
```

```{r}
  "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[2],

)

analysis_data_360 <- rich_features_final_360 %>%

  select(Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, 
         Instability, Learning_Rate) %>%
  scale()

set.seed(123)
k_global_360 <- kmeans(global_input_360, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
analysis_data_360$Global_Cluster <- as.factor(k_global_360$cluster)

cluster_stats_360 <- analysis_data_360 %>%
  group_by(Global_Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_ability = mean(ability),
    mean_slope   = mean(Rel_Slope), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

low_eff_id_360 <- cluster_stats_360 %>%
  arrange(mean_ability) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)

effective_clusters_360 <- cluster_stats_360 %>%
  filter(Global_Cluster != low_eff_id_360) %>%
  arrange(mean_slope)

analytical_id_360 <- effective_clusters_360 %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)
holistic_id_360   <- effective_clusters_360 %>% slice(2) %>% pull(Global_Cluster)

analysis_data_360 <- analysis_data_360 %>%
  mutate(Strategy_Label = case_when(
    Global_Cluster == low_eff_id_360    ~ "Ineffective Strategies",
    Global_Cluster == analytical_id_360 ~ "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)",
    Global_Cluster == holistic_id_360   ~ "Mental Rotation"
  ))

  )
```

####################### ROBUSTNESS CHECK - BOOTSTRAPPING ##########################
```{r}
#| label: cluster-stability-bootstrap
#| include: false
#| eval: false

vars   <- c("Baseline_Speed", "Rel_Slope", "Abs_Slope", "Instability", "Learning_Rate")
k      <- 3
B      <- 500
nstart <- 25
set.seed(123)

df_full <- analysis_data %>%
  select(user_id, Strategy_Label, all_of(vars)) %>%
  distinct(user_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(if_all(all_of(vars), is.finite)) %>%
  mutate(
    Strategy_Label = factor(
      Strategy_Label,
      levels = names(my_colors)   
    )
  )

stopifnot(nlevels(df_full$Strategy_Label) == 3)
stopifnot(n_distinct(df_full$user_id) == nrow(df_full))

ref_levels <- levels(df_full$Strategy_Label)
y_ref      <- df_full$Strategy_Label
ids        <- df_full$user_id
n          <- nrow(df_full)

# scaling: lock to full-sample mean/sd so bootstrap runs are comparable
mu  <- df_full %>% summarise(across(all_of(vars), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))) %>% as.list()
sdv <- df_full %>% summarise(across(all_of(vars), \(x) sd(x,   na.rm = TRUE))) %>% as.list()

X_full <- df_full %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(vars), ~ (. - mu[[cur_column()]]) / sdv[[cur_column()]])) %>%
  select(all_of(vars)) %>%
  as.matrix()

# helpers
ARI <- function(a, b) {
  a <- as.integer(factor(a))
  b <- as.integer(factor(b))
  tab <- table(a, b)
  n <- sum(tab)
  if (n <= 1) return(NA_real_)
  comb2    <- function(x) x * (x - 1) / 2
  sum_ij   <- sum(comb2(tab))
  sum_i    <- sum(comb2(rowSums(tab)))
  sum_j    <- sum(comb2(colSums(tab)))
  expected <- (sum_i * sum_j) / comb2(n)
  max_idx  <- 0.5 * (sum_i + sum_j)
  denom    <- max_idx - expected
  if (denom == 0) return(NA_real_)
  (sum_ij - expected) / denom
}

jaccard <- function(set_a, set_b) {
  inter <- length(intersect(set_a, set_b))
  uni   <- length(union(set_a, set_b))
  if (uni == 0) NA_real_ else inter / uni
}

all_perms_3 <- list(
  c(1,2,3), c(1,3,2),
  c(2,1,3), c(2,3,1),
  c(3,1,2), c(3,2,1)
)

# Match bootstrap cluster IDs to reference labels by maximum membership overlap
best_perm_by_overlap <- function(cl_hat, y_ref, ref_levels, all_perms_3) {
  tab    <- table(cl_hat, factor(y_ref, levels = ref_levels))
  scores <- sapply(all_perms_3, function(p) sum(tab[cbind(1:3, p)]))
  all_perms_3[[which.max(scores)]]
}

# reference k-means (reproduces clustering-execution exactly)
# UPDATED: label assignment now mirrors the two-step logic in clustering-execution:
#   step 1 — lowest mean ability  → "Ineffective Strategies"
#   step 2 — of the remainder, flatter Rel_Slope → "Other Effective...", 
#             steeper → "Mental Rotation"
# We use this to build ref_centers aligned to ref_levels.

# need ability for label assignment (not a clustering var, so grab separately)
ability_lookup <- df_full %>%
  left_join(analysis_data %>% distinct(user_id, ability), by = "user_id")

set.seed(123)
km_ref <- kmeans(X_full, centers = k, nstart = nstart)
cl_ref <- km_ref$cluster

# replicate the production label-assignment rule on the reference run
cluster_stats_ref <- tibble(
  cluster      = 1:k,
  mean_ability = tapply(ability_lookup$ability, cl_ref, mean, na.rm = TRUE),
  mean_rel_slope = tapply(df_full$Rel_Slope,   cl_ref, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
)

low_eff_id_ref  <- cluster_stats_ref %>% arrange(mean_ability) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(cluster)
effective_ref   <- cluster_stats_ref %>% filter(cluster != low_eff_id_ref) %>% arrange(mean_rel_slope)
analytical_id_ref <- effective_ref %>% slice(1) %>% pull(cluster)
holistic_id_ref   <- effective_ref %>% slice(2) %>% pull(cluster)

# map cluster integer to ref_levels index (used to order ref_centers rows)
label_order_ref <- integer(k)
label_order_ref[low_eff_id_ref]   <- which(ref_levels == "Ineffective Strategies")
label_order_ref[analytical_id_ref] <- which(ref_levels == "Other Effective Strategies (Feature matching/Flipping)")
label_order_ref[holistic_id_ref]   <- which(ref_levels == "Mental Rotation")

# ref_centers[i, ] corresponds to ref_levels[i]
ref_centers <- km_ref$centers[order(label_order_ref), , drop = FALSE]

# bootstrap loop
res <- map_dfr(1:B, function(b) {

  set.seed(1000 + b)

  idx        <- sample.int(n, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  idx_unique <- unique(idx)

  tab_ref_unique <- table(factor(y_ref[idx_unique], levels = ref_levels))
  min_ref_unique <- min(tab_ref_unique)
  min_ref_prop   <- min_ref_unique / length(idx_unique)
  n_unique       <- length(idx_unique)

  X_b <- X_full[idx, , drop = FALSE]
  km  <- kmeans(X_b, centers = k, nstart = nstart)

  # assign all full-sample participants to nearest bootstrap center
  centers_b <- km$centers
  dists <- sapply(1:k, function(j) {
    rowSums((X_full - matrix(centers_b[j, ],
                             nrow = nrow(X_full), ncol = ncol(X_full),
                             byrow = TRUE))^2)
  })
  cl_hat <- max.col(-dists)

  # resolve label switching via maximum overlap with reference labels
  perm  <- best_perm_by_overlap(cl_hat, y_ref, ref_levels, all_perms_3)
  y_hat <- factor(ref_levels[perm[cl_hat]], levels = ref_levels)

  ari <- ARI(y_ref, y_hat)

  # per-cluster Jaccard
  jac <- map_dbl(ref_levels, function(lab) {
    jaccard(ids[y_ref == lab], ids[y_hat == lab])
  })
  names(jac) <- paste0("J_", make.names(ref_levels))

  # mean centroid displacement vs reference
  centers_b_aligned <- centers_b[perm, , drop = FALSE]
  center_shift      <- mean(sqrt(rowSums((centers_b_aligned - ref_centers)^2)))

  tibble(
    replicate      = b,
    ARI            = ari,
    n_unique       = n_unique,
    min_ref_unique = min_ref_unique,
    min_ref_prop   = min_ref_prop,
    center_shift   = center_shift,
    !!!as.list(jac)
  )
})

# summaries
stability_summary <- res %>%
  summarise(
    B                   = n(),
    ARI_median          = median(ARI, na.rm = TRUE),
    ARI_IQR             = IQR(ARI, na.rm = TRUE),
    center_shift_median = median(center_shift, na.rm = TRUE),
    center_shift_IQR    = IQR(center_shift, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(starts_with("J_"),
           list(median = ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
                IQR    = ~ IQR(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
  )

stability_summary

ari_tail <- res %>%
  summarise(
    pct_ARI_below_0.70 = mean(ARI < 0.70, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_ARI_below_0.60 = mean(ARI < 0.60, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    min_ARI            = min(ARI, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ari_tail
```

####################### ROBUSTNESS CHECK - WITHIN PERSON STRATEGY SWITCHING (DORIA'S ANALYSIS) ##########################

### Strategy Stability Analysis (Split-Half Reliability)

To investigate whether children consistently use a single cognitive strategy throughout the task or switch strategies over time (e.g., discovering a shortcut), we performed a **Split-Half Reliability Analysis**.

**Methodology:**
We partitioned each participant's data into two sequential halves: the first 50% of trials (Early Phase) and the last 50% of trials (Late Phase). For each half, we estimated a "Raw Slope" using a simple linear regression of reaction time on angle (`log_rt ~ angle`). This slope serves as a proxy for the participant's rotation strategy during that specific period. 

We then correlated the *First Half Slope* with the *Second Half Slope* to quantify stability. A high correlation ($r \approx 1$) would indicate a fixed strategy, while a low correlation ($r \approx 0$) suggests dynamic behavior or strategy switching.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strategy-switching
#| fig-cap: "Strategy Stability: Comparison of Rotation Slope in First Half vs. Second Half of trials. Points below the diagonal suggest a switch to a flatter strategy (e.g., discovering the shortcut)."
#| eval: false

# 1. Split Data into Halves
# We determine the midpoint trial for each user
split_data <- mrot_rich_data %>%
  group_by(user_id) %>%
  mutate(
    Midpoint = median(trial_number, na.rm = TRUE),
    Half = ifelse(trial_number <= Midpoint, "First_Half", "Second_Half")
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Filter out bad data points just to be safe
  filter(is.finite(log_rt), is.finite(angle))

# 2. Calculate Simple Slope for Each Half (Using simple lm per subject)
# This is a fast proxy for the complex mixed-model slope
slope_stability <- split_data %>%
  group_by(user_id, Half) %>%
  summarise(
    # We only care about the slope (coefficient for angle)
    # We use a safe lm() call wrapped in tryCatch to handle kids with too few trials
    Raw_Slope = tryCatch(
      #coef(lm(log_rt ~ angle, data = pick(everything())))["angle"], 
      # Use distance from 0 so the slope represents 'cost of rotation'
  coef(lm(log_rt ~ pmin(angle, 360 - angle), data = pick(everything())))[2],
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Reshape to Wide Format (Columns: Slope_First, Slope_Second)
  pivot_wider(names_from = Half, values_from = Raw_Slope, names_prefix = "Slope_") %>%
  # Join with our Final Strategy Labels to color-code
  left_join(analysis_data %>% select(user_id, Strategy_Label), by = "user_id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Label), !is.na(Slope_First_Half), !is.na(Slope_Second_Half))

# 3. Calculate Correlation (Quantify Stability)
correlation <- cor(slope_stability$Slope_First_Half, slope_stability$Slope_Second_Half, use = "complete.obs")

# 4. Visualization
ggplot(slope_stability, aes(x = Slope_First_Half, y = Slope_Second_Half, color = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") + # The "Stability Line"
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Strategy Switching Check (Split-Half Reliability)",
    subtitle = paste0("Correlation between halves: r = ", round(correlation, 2), 
                      ". Points below diagonal = Strategy became flatter (faster)."),
    x = "Slope (First Half of Trials)",
    y = "Slope (Second Half of Trials)"
  ) +
  coord_fixed() # Keeps the aspect ratio square so the diagonal is 45 degrees
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Doria's original code for examining up to 360 
mrot_rich_data <- mrot_rt_trial %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus = str_extract(item, "^[a-z]+"),
    
    # 1. Extract the base angle (e.g., 40)
    base_angle = as.integer(str_extract(item, "\\d+")), 
    
    # 2. Detect if the original item was a "Negative/Counter-Clockwise" rotation
    # Looking for 'rn' prefix in item_original (e.g., rn040)
    is_ccw = str_detect(item_original, "^rn"),
    
    # 3. RECONSTRUCT the full 0-360 angle
    angle = ifelse(is_ccw, 360 - base_angle, base_angle),
    
    # 4. Calculate shortest distance to center (disparity) for the model
    # This ensures the model still measures 'Rotation Cost' correctly
    ang_disparity = pmin(angle, 360 - angle),
    
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    # SCALE THE DISPARITY, NOT THE RAW ANGLE
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(ang_disparity)), 
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

#  Issues: the above code is only only catches rabbit counter-clockwise items (rn040, rn080 etc.), and misses duck and shape items. It is also not necessary to deconstruct item_original as the info. we need is already there. item_original already contains the full angle directly (e.g., an11240 = 240).
```
